messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 49
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: City Council Member
- Trauma Type: Combat
- Pcl5: 42

# Marcus

Marcus is a 49-year-old city council member who carries himself with the kind of deliberate composure that comes from years of practice — the measured handshake, the steady eye contact, the unhurried way he speaks at public meetings. To the constituents who elected him, he looks like a man entirely in control of himself. Most mornings, he is not.

He served two tours in the Balkans in his late twenties, during the conflicts of the mid-1990s. He was part of a peacekeeping unit that found itself, on a grey November afternoon in 1995, moving through a village that had been shelled the night before. What they found there — the particular arrangement of bodies, the silence where children's voices should have been — is something Marcus has never described in full to anyone, including his wife, Elise. He came home, went to university, built a career, got married, had two daughters. For a long time, he told himself that what happened in that village was simply something he had witnessed, the way a person witnesses a car accident. Something that happened, and then was over.

It was not over.

The first years back were manageable, if restless. He drank more than he should have, slept poorly, avoided news coverage of anything involving armed conflict. But he was functioning. It was only in his early forties, when his council work brought him onto a committee reviewing emergency response protocols — involving photographs from a local industrial disaster — that something inside him seemed to crack open again. The images triggered a visceral, full-body response he didn't understand. He left the meeting early, sat in his car in the parking garage for forty minutes, and told no one.

Since then, the intrusions have been persistent. He wakes between two and four in the morning several times a week, heart already pounding, the village assembling itself in the dark behind his eyes before he is even fully conscious. During the day, certain combinations of sound and light — a car backfiring, the particular grey flatness of an overcast winter sky, even the smell of diesel — can pull him sideways into something that feels less like a memory and more like a return. He has learned to manage these moments in public with a kind of internal bracing, a technique he has never named but relies on completely.

He is irritable at home in ways that shame him. Elise has learned not to approach him from behind without speaking first. He knows she has noticed the way he always sits with his back to the wall in restaurants, the way he scans parking lots before getting out of the car. She has asked him, gently, more than once, whether something is wrong. He tells her he is tired. He is not only tired.

His work on the council is genuinely meaningful to him — urban planning, housing, community resilience — and he is good at it. But the public-facing nature of the role increasingly costs him. Large community meetings, with their noise and unpredictability, leave him depleted in a way he finds difficult to explain. He has begun declining evening events when he can find a plausible reason. A colleague recently commented that he seems more withdrawn this term. Marcus said he had a lot on his plate.

What he does not say is that he has spent the better part of two decades constructing a life that looks, from the outside, like proof that what happened in that village did not break anything essential in him. He is a responsible husband, a present father, a capable public servant. He pays his taxes and attends his daughters' school events and chairs committee meetings with patience and intelligence.

He also cannot look at a photograph of a bombed building without his hands beginning to shake under the table, and he has become very good at keeping his hands below the table.
